screens.title: Lists and Sets
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we step into two foundational collection interfaces in Java: List and Set. You'll learn what it means for a collection to be ordered versus unique, why some implementations are better for random access and others for quick insertions, and how equality and ordering rules affect behavior in sets. We will use concrete examples: an enrollment playlist to show how a List preserves duplicates and position, and a student registry to show how a Set enforces uniqueness. You will also see how implementation details — an array, a linked list, a hash table or a red-black tree — change performance characteristics for get, add, and remove operations. By the end, you will know which implementation to pick when you need fast lookup, stable insertion order, or sorted traversal, and you will understand the common pitfall where incorrect equals and hashCode produce duplicated entries in a HashSet. Think of this lesson as a practical decision guide that links abstract interfaces to concrete code and runtime trade-offs. Start by seeing three central topics we will explore: List implementations, Set implementations, and object equality and ordering.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: This chapter sets five practical objectives you will reach by working through examples and code. First, you will be able to distinguish List from Set by their rules for ordering and duplicates; that helps you pick a structure for playlists or unique registries. Second, you'll compare ArrayList and LinkedList, learning when dynamic arrays outperform linked nodes and vice versa, and why get by index is constant time in one and linear in the other. Third, you'll compare HashSet, LinkedHashSet and TreeSet, understanding hash tables, insertion-order maintenance, and red-black tree sorting so you can choose between raw speed, predictable order, or sorted traversal. Fourth, you'll implement hashCode and equals correctly for custom objects so HashSet and HashMap recognize duplicates and avoid subtle bugs. Finally, you'll use Comparable and Comparator to define natural and custom ordering in TreeSet and TreeMap. Each objective emphasizes a concrete coding skill plus the reasoning behind it, so you can both write correct code and explain why a particular implementation fits your use case.

screens.title: The List interface
screens.narratorSegment: A List in Java is an ordered collection where each element has a position and can be accessed by an integer index. That ordering is guaranteed by the interface: insertions add elements at specific positions, and duplicates are allowed. A helpful everyday analogy is a playlist of songs: the same song can appear more than once and its position matters. Lists support index-based operations such as get, set, add at index, and remove by index. These operations are implemented differently by concrete classes that back the list — for example, an ArrayList uses a dynamic array, while a LinkedList uses node references. That implementation choice changes performance: array-backed lists offer constant-time random access, while node-based lists offer constant-time insertions at the ends. Common misconceptions arise when beginners assume all List implementations have the same performance. The right mental model is to treat List as a contract — positional access and duplicates allowed — and then examine implementations for performance when you need to optimize. A short example you will practice is maintaining enrollment order with an ArrayList when you often read entries by index, and choosing a linked structure when you need cheap head or tail insertions.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › The List interface

The List interface

Ordered collections with positional access and duplicates allowed.

Definition
What a List guarantees
  • Elements have a well-defined order and can be accessed by index.
  • Duplicate elements are allowed; equality is by equals unless otherwise specified.
  • Supports positional operations: add(index), remove(index), get(index), set(index, element).
Analogy
A playlist where order and repeats matter.
Example operations
List names = new ArrayList<>();
names.add("Alice");
names.add("Bob");
names.add(1, "Charlie"); // insert at index 1
String first = names.get(0); // read by index
names.remove(2); // remove by index
System.out.println(names);
Code: dynamic array backed list example. Observe insert and get semantics.
Key takeaway
Pick a List for ordered, indexable sequences; check implementation for expected performance.
Common mistake
Assuming get(index) is fast for all Lists; it is O(1) for ArrayList but O(n) for LinkedList.
Pro tip
If you need deque behavior, LinkedList implements Deque and may be more convenient for head/tail operations.

screens.title: ArrayList deep dive
screens.narratorSegment: ArrayList is the go-to List implementation because it is backed by a resizable array. Conceptually, elements are stored in contiguous memory like entries in an array. This layout gives constant time random access: a call to get(index) is a direct array lookup. Adding to the end is usually amortized constant time: when capacity remains, append is O(1); if the backing array needs to grow, the array is copied to a larger block and that insertion becomes O(n) for that operation. Insertions or removals in the middle require shifting elements and thus cost O(n). Because of this behavior, ArrayList is best when you do frequent indexed reads and append operations but few middle insertions. A common misconception is to choose ArrayList because of familiarity without measuring expected insertion patterns; in scenarios where you frequently insert at the front or remove from both ends, a linked structure may be faster. Practically, use ArrayList for ordered buffers, result lists from queries, or when implementing random-access algorithms where indexing is common. We'll show a small code example illustrating add, get and remove and then compare timings conceptually so you can reason about trade-offs in real apps.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › ArrayList deep dive

ArrayList deep dive

Dynamic array: fast random access, shifting on middle edits.

Implementation
Behavior & costs
  • get(index): O(1) — direct array access.
  • add(element) at end: amortized O(1); occasional O(n) when resizing.
  • add/remove in middle: O(n) due to element shifting.
Use case
When random access dominates and middle edits are rare.
Code example
List arrayList = new ArrayList<>();
arrayList.add("Apple");
arrayList.add("Banana");
arrayList.add(1, "Cherry"); // O(n) shift when inserting at index
String fruit = arrayList.get(0); // O(1)
arrayList.remove(1); // O(n) shift when removing
Note: resizing copies the backing array to a larger array when capacity is exceeded.
Key takeaway
Prefer ArrayList for indexed reads and append-heavy workloads.
Misconception
Assuming ArrayList is always faster than LinkedList; performance depends on operation types.
Try this
Measure small benchmarks for your expected workloads before optimizing prematurely.

screens.title: LinkedList deep dive
screens.narratorSegment: LinkedList implements List using a doubly-linked node structure. Each node contains references to the previous and next nodes, so adding or removing elements at the ends is constant time. This is why LinkedList is often chosen for queue or deque usages: addFirst, addLast, removeFirst and removeLast are O(1). However, random access by index is slow because the list must be traversed from the head or tail until the desired index is reached; get(index) is O(n). Insertions or removals in the middle are efficient once you've located the node, but locating that node costs O(n) traversal time. A typical use case is an event queue where you frequently push and pop at the ends. A common mistake is to use LinkedList when you need many indexed reads — in that case ArrayList is better. LinkedList also implements Deque, giving you direct access to deque methods useful for stack and queue patterns. When reasoning about memory, understand LinkedList has node overhead per element, which matters for very large lists. Always match the expected operation profile to the data structure to avoid hidden O(n) costs.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › LinkedList deep dive

LinkedList deep dive

Doubly-linked structure: great for edge insertions and deque operations.

Implementation
Behavior & costs
  • addFirst/addLast/removeFirst/removeLast: O(1).
  • get(index): O(n) due to traversal from head or tail.
  • Insert/remove in middle: O(1) once node found, but node lookup cost is O(n).
Use case
When you need frequent head or tail updates or a Deque API.
Example operations
LinkedList list = new LinkedList<>();
list.add("Dog");
list.add("Elephant");
list.addFirst("Cat"); // O(1)
String first = list.get(0); // O(n) traversal
list.removeFirst(); // O(1)
Note: useful as a Deque for queue/stack behaviors without array resizing costs.
Key takeaway
Choose LinkedList for cheap end insertions and Deque patterns, not for random-access-heavy code.
Misconception
Expecting LinkedList to be memory-light; each element stores extra node references increasing overhead.
Pro tip
For mixed workloads, benchmark both implementations with representative data sizes.

screens.title: ArrayList vs LinkedList
screens.narratorSegment: When choosing between ArrayList and LinkedList, focus on the operations you will do most. If you primarily access elements by index, ArrayList gives constant time reads and will usually be faster due to locality of reference. If you mostly insert or remove elements at the ends, LinkedList offers constant-time additions and removals without shifting. For middle insertions, ArrayList pays a linear cost for shifting, while LinkedList pays the linear cost to find the node plus an O(1) relink; the net effect often favors ArrayList unless your application consistently manipulates nodes near the ends. Another practical factor is memory: LinkedList stores node objects with two references per element, increasing overhead; ArrayList stores primitives and object references contiguously, which can be more compact. A common pitfall is using LinkedList with lots of indexed get calls — its traversal cost can dramatically slow the program. Measure realistic workloads and remember that algorithmic complexity and constant factors both matter for production code. ArrayList vs LinkedList means match the collection to your dominant operations: random access → arraylist; frequent end insertions/removals → linkedlist.. In practical terms, operation cost comparison and practical selection rules. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Compare operation costs and pick by dominant workload.

Comparison

screens.title: The Set interface
screens.narratorSegment: A Set is a collection that contains no duplicate elements. If you attempt to add an element that is already present, the add operation usually returns false and the collection remains unchanged. Sets do not guarantee order in their general contract, but individual implementations provide different ordering behaviors — for example, insertion order or sorted order. Use a Set when uniqueness is required, such as tracking unique IDs, visited nodes, or user registrations where duplicates would be incorrect. When storing custom objects, membership and duplication depend on how equality is defined. For hash-based sets, correct equals and hashCode implementations are essential. For sorted sets, Comparable or a Comparator must be provided so the set can order elements and identify duplicates according to the comparison. Confusing identity equality (object reference) with logical equality is a common beginner mistake; always decide which fields of your object determine uniqueness and implement equality consistently with that choice. The Set interface means set = no duplicates; ordering depends on implementation; equality rules determine membership.. In practical terms, collections that enforce uniqueness. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › The Set interface

The Set interface

Collections that prevent duplicates. Order is implementation-dependent.

Definition
Set guarantees
  • No duplicate elements as defined by equality rules.
  • Order is not part of the Set contract; implementations may preserve insertion order or sort elements.
  • Choice of Set implementation affects performance and traversal behavior.
Analogy
A guestlist where each person must be unique; duplicates are not allowed.
When to use a Set
  • Ensure uniqueness of identifiers or keys.
  • Fast membership tests when using hash-based sets.
  • Sorted traversal when using tree-based sets.
Decide whether you need insertion-order, hashing performance, or sorted order, then pick an implementation.
Key takeaway
Use Set when uniqueness matters; choose implementation based on ordering and performance needs.
Common error
Relying on default object identity rather than logical equality when deciding uniqueness.
Pro tip
Always document which fields determine equality when designing a class used in sets.

screens.title: HashSet and the equals/hashCode contract
screens.narratorSegment: HashSet stores elements in buckets determined by their hash codes. When you add an object, the set computes its hash code to find the target bucket. If the bucket contains items with the same hash code, the set uses equals to check for true equality and avoid duplicates. This two-stage check — hashCode first, equals second — is why you must override both methods consistently for custom classes. If equals returns true but hashCode returns different values, the collection can place equal objects in different buckets and treat them as distinct, causing duplicates. Conversely, equal hash codes with a correctly implemented equals keeps correctness while allowing collisions. A concrete example is a Product class that uses name and price to compute hash and equals. We'll walk through a small code snippet showing equals and hashCode implemented with Objects. hash, then show how HashSet behaves when you add logically equal products. A common misconception is to override equals only; that breaks hashed collections. The takeaway: equals and hashCode form a contract—implement both based on the same fields. HashSet and the equals/hashCode contract means for hashset to work, equals and hashcode must be consistent: equal objects must have equal hash codes.. In practical terms, why equals and hashcode must agree for hash-based collections. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › hashCode & equals

HashSet and equals/hashCode

Hash-based membership relies on a consistent equality contract.

Code walkthrough
Product equality example
class Product {
  private String name;
  private double price;

  // constructor, getters omitted

  @Override
  public boolean equals(Object o) {
    if (this == o) return true;
    if (o == null || getClass() != o.getClass()) return false;
    Product p = (Product) o;
    return Double.compare(p.price, price) == 0 && Objects.equals(name, p.name);
  }

  @Override
  public int hashCode() {
    return Objects.hash(name, price);
  }
}
When two Product instances have the same name and price, equals returns true and hashCode returns the same int so HashSet treats them as duplicates.
Key takeaway
Always override both equals and hashCode using the same fields for equality.
Common bug
Overriding equals without hashCode leads to incorrect HashSet or HashMap behavior and mysterious duplicates or lookups that fail.
Example test
Add two equal products to a HashSet; it should contain only one instance after both adds.

screens.title: LinkedHashSet and TreeSet
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond HashSet, Java provides specialized Set implementations that give different ordering guarantees. LinkedHashSet keeps a linked list of entries to preserve insertion order; it offers near-constant-time operations with a small overhead compared to HashSet. Use LinkedHashSet when you need uniqueness and a predictable traversal order that matches insertion. TreeSet stores elements in a balanced binary search tree, specifically a red-black tree, providing sorted order for iteration and log(n) time for add, remove and contains. TreeSet requires elements implement Comparable or for you to supply a Comparator at construction. TreeSet is excellent when you need range operations like headSet or tailSet and consistent sorted iteration. Keep in mind the performance trade-off: TreeSet's log(n) costs are higher than hash-based O(1) in average cases but give ordering and range query support. screens.title: Comparable vs Comparator
screens.narratorSegment: Sorting in Java can be done two ways for custom classes. Implementing Comparable gives a single natural ordering via compareTo; the class carries its own ordering logic. Code example
compareTo example
@Override
public int compareTo(Product other) {
  int nameComparison = this.name.compareTo(other.name);

Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Student class

Student class for roster

Make equality and ordering explicit so sets behave predictably.

Code walkthrough
Student implementation (expected structure)
class Student implements Comparable {
  private String id;
  private String name;

  public Student(String id, String name) { this.id = id; this.name = name; }
  public String getId() { return id; }
  public String getName() { return name; }

  @Override
  public String toString() { return "Student{id='" + id + "', name='" + name + "'}"; }

  @Override
  public boolean equals(Object o) {
    if (this == o) return true;
    if (o == null || getClass() != o.getClass()) return false;
    Student s = (Student) o;
    return Objects.equals(id, s.id) && Objects.equals(name, s.name);
  }

  @Override
  public int hashCode() { return Objects.hash(id, name); }

  @Override
  public int compareTo(Student other) {
    int nameCmp = this.name.compareTo(other.name);
    if (nameCmp != 0) return nameCmp;
    return this.id.compareTo(other.id);
  }
}
Add identical Student instances to an ArrayList, HashSet and TreeSet to observe differing results: duplicates remain in ArrayList, are removed in HashSet, and sorted/unique in TreeSet.

Make equality and ordering explicit in the class used by sets and sorted sets.

Verify that equals, hashCode and compareTo use the same identity fields where appropriate.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we step into two foundational collection interfaces in Java: List and Set. You'll learn what it means for a collection to be ordered versus unique, why some implementations are better for random access and others for quick insertions, and how equality and ordering rules affect behavior in sets. We will use concrete examples: an enrollment playlist to show how a List preserves duplicates and position, and a student registry to show how a Set enforces uniqueness. You will also see how implementation details — an array, a linked list, a hash table or a red-black tree — change performance characteristics for get, add, and remove operations. By the end, you will know which implementation to pick when you need fast lookup, stable insertion order, or sorted traversal, and you will understand the common pitfall where incorrect equals and hashCode produce duplicated entries in a HashSet. Think of this lesson as a practical decision guide that links abstract interfaces to concrete code and runtime trade-offs. Start by seeing three central topics we will explore: List implementations, Set implementations, and object equality and ordering.

This chapter sets five practical objectives you will reach by working through examples and code. First, you will be able to distinguish List from Set by their rules for ordering and duplicates; that helps you pick a structure for playlists or unique registries. Second, you'll compare ArrayList and LinkedList, learning when dynamic arrays outperform linked nodes and vice versa, and why get by index is constant time in one and linear in the other. Third, you'll compare HashSet, LinkedHashSet and TreeSet, understanding hash tables, insertion-order maintenance, and red-black tree sorting so you can choose between raw speed, predictable order, or sorted traversal. Fourth, you'll implement hashCode and equals correctly for custom objects so HashSet and HashMap recognize duplicates and avoid subtle bugs. Finally, you'll use Comparable and Comparator to define natural and custom ordering in TreeSet and TreeMap. Each objective emphasizes a concrete coding skill plus the reasoning behind it, so you can both write correct code and explain why a particular implementation fits your use case.

This second objectives slide focuses on applying knowledge through examples and code. You will practice selecting the right collection for particular needs: preserving insertion order with LinkedHashSet, enforcing uniqueness with HashSet, and retrieving sorted elements with TreeSet. You will implement equals and hashCode together so hashed collections detect duplicates correctly; a common bug is to override equals but not hashCode, which breaks set membership. You will also practice Comparable and Comparator to control ordering in TreeSet and TreeMap, learning when to use a natural ordering versus an external comparator. Each objective ties to an actionable milestone: write a small Student class, run a roster example with ArrayList, HashSet and TreeSet, and observe the differences. These checks make the learning measurable: can you explain why duplicate entries appear or why sorted output differs? Being able to answer those questions means you can pick the right structure in the real systems you build.

A List in Java is an ordered collection where each element has a position and can be accessed by an integer index. That ordering is guaranteed by the interface: insertions add elements at specific positions, and duplicates are allowed. A helpful everyday analogy is a playlist of songs: the same song can appear more than once and its position matters. Lists support index-based operations such as get, set, add at index, and remove by index. These operations are implemented differently by concrete classes that back the list — for example, an ArrayList uses a dynamic array, while a LinkedList uses node references. That implementation choice changes performance: array-backed lists offer constant-time random access, while node-based lists offer constant-time insertions at the ends. Common misconceptions arise when beginners assume all List implementations have the same performance. The right mental model is to treat List as a contract — positional access and duplicates allowed — and then examine implementations for performance when you need to optimize. A short example you will practice is maintaining enrollment order with an ArrayList when you often read entries by index, and choosing a linked structure when you need cheap head or tail insertions.

ArrayList is the go-to List implementation because it is backed by a resizable array. Conceptually, elements are stored in contiguous memory like entries in an array. This layout gives constant time random access: a call to get(index) is a direct array lookup. Adding to the end is usually amortized constant time: when capacity remains, append is O(1); if the backing array needs to grow, the array is copied to a larger block and that insertion becomes O(n) for that operation. Insertions or removals in the middle require shifting elements and thus cost O(n). Because of this behavior, ArrayList is best when you do frequent indexed reads and append operations but few middle insertions. A common misconception is to choose ArrayList because of familiarity without measuring expected insertion patterns; in scenarios where you frequently insert at the front or remove from both ends, a linked structure may be faster. Practically, use ArrayList for ordered buffers, result lists from queries, or when implementing random-access algorithms where indexing is common. We'll show a small code example illustrating add, get and remove and then compare timings conceptually so you can reason about trade-offs in real apps.

LinkedList implements List using a doubly-linked node structure. Each node contains references to the previous and next nodes, so adding or removing elements at the ends is constant time. This is why LinkedList is often chosen for queue or deque usages: addFirst, addLast, removeFirst and removeLast are O(1). However, random access by index is slow because the list must be traversed from the head or tail until the desired index is reached; get(index) is O(n). Insertions or removals in the middle are efficient once you've located the node, but locating that node costs O(n) traversal time. A typical use case is an event queue where you frequently push and pop at the ends. A common mistake is to use LinkedList when you need many indexed reads — in that case ArrayList is better. LinkedList also implements Deque, giving you direct access to deque methods useful for stack and queue patterns. When reasoning about memory, understand LinkedList has node overhead per element, which matters for very large lists. Always match the expected operation profile to the data structure to avoid hidden O(n) costs.

When choosing between ArrayList and LinkedList, focus on the operations you will do most. If you primarily access elements by index, ArrayList gives constant time reads and will usually be faster due to locality of reference. If you mostly insert or remove elements at the ends, LinkedList offers constant-time additions and removals without shifting. For middle insertions, ArrayList pays a linear cost for shifting, while LinkedList pays the linear cost to find the node plus an O(1) relink; the net effect often favors ArrayList unless your application consistently manipulates nodes near the ends. Another practical factor is memory: LinkedList stores node objects with two references per element, increasing overhead; ArrayList stores primitives and object references contiguously, which can be more compact. A common pitfall is using LinkedList with lots of indexed get calls — its traversal cost can dramatically slow the program. Measure realistic workloads and remember that algorithmic complexity and constant factors both matter for production code. For performance, start by identifying the dominant operations: reads by index, append, head/tail insertions, or membership tests.
